title: Abram and Lot Part Ways
summary: Abram returns from Egypt to the altar near Bethel, rich in livestock, silver, and gold. His flocks and Lot's are too large for the land to support together, and their herdsmen quarrel, so Abram offers Lot his choice of the land. Lot chooses the well-watered plain of the Jordan and settles near Sodom, whose people are wicked. The LORD then tells Abram to look in every direction, promises him all the land he sees and offspring as countless as the dust, and Abram settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
story: The detour into Egypt in chapter 12 left Abram wealthy but compromised. Chapter 13 shows him going back to where he started, to the altar between Bethel and Ai, and calling on the LORD again. The wealth he brought from Egypt now creates a new problem, a quarrel with his nephew Lot. How Abram handles it shows a man learning to trust God's promise instead of grasping. Lot's choice sets up the stories to come: his capture in chapter 14 and the destruction of Sodom in chapter 19. And the LORD's renewed promise, given right after Lot leaves, moves the story toward the covenant of chapter 15. The question hanging over the chapter is who will inherit the land. Lot took what looked best; God gives Abram all of it.
historical:
The chapter takes place in the central hill country of Canaan, around Bethel and Ai, north of Jerusalem, and then at Hebron in the southern hills. From the ridge near Bethel a person can look east over the Jordan valley, which fits Lot's view of the plain. The plain of the Jordan (in Hebrew, the kikkar, the round or circle) refers to the broad, well-watered valley of the Jordan near the Dead Sea. The location of Sodom, Gomorrah, and the other cities of the plain is debated. Traditionally they have been placed near the southern end of the Dead Sea, where Zoar is usually located; some scholars have argued for sites on the plain north of the Dead Sea, across from Jericho. No identification has won general agreement.

The Canaanites and Perizzites were living in the land (verse 7). The Perizzites are known only from the Bible; their name may be related to a word for open, unwalled villages, which would describe rural dwellers rather than a distinct ethnic group. Hebron, where Abram settles, was an ancient town in the hills south of Jerusalem. It will become the family burial place (chapter 23) and much later David's first capital.
cultural:
Herdsmen in the ancient Near East needed pasture and water, both scarce in the hill country, and quarrels over wells and grazing land were common (see 21:25 and 26:20). When the flocks of two households grew large, separation was the practical solution. What is striking is the way Abram does it. As the elder and the head of the family, custom would have given him the right to choose first. Instead he gives Lot the choice. His words, we are brothers, use the broad Hebrew sense of the word for a close relative, and they appeal to family loyalty over property.

The comparison of the Jordan plain to the garden of the LORD and the land of Egypt would have meant a great deal to readers in Canaan, a land that depended on rain. Eden was watered by rivers, and Egypt by the Nile, so both stood for abundance that did not depend on the sky. The LORD's command to Abram to walk through the length and breadth of the land may reflect an ancient way of symbolically claiming territory; God later tells Joshua, “I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread” (Joshua 1:3).
literary: The chapter is built around two acts of looking. In verse 10, Lot lifted up his eyes and saw that the plain was well watered, and he chose it for himself. The language recalls Eve, who saw that the tree was good and pleasing to the eyes (3:6), and the comparison to the garden of the LORD deepens the echo. Then in verse 14, after Lot has gone, the LORD tells Abram to lift up his eyes and look in every direction, and promises that all he sees will be given to him. Lot chooses by sight; Abram receives by promise. The narrator adds warning signs to Lot's choice: the parenthesis that this was before the LORD destroyed Sodom, the note that Lot moved east (in Genesis, the direction of departure from Eden, of Cain's exile, and of the settlers at Babel), the gradual drift as he pitched his tent toward Sodom, and the blunt comment that the men of Sodom were wicked. The chapter begins and ends at an altar, framing Abram's life with worship.

outline.t: Abram returns to the altar near Bethel
Too many flocks and a quarrel among herdsmen
Lot chooses the Jordan plain and settles near Sodom
The LORD promises Abram the land and countless offspring
Abram settles at Hebron and builds an altar

doctrines.note: God repeats and enlarges his promise: all the land Abram can see, given to him and his offspring forever, and offspring as uncountable as the dust of the earth. The promise comes right after Abram has given up his claim to choose, showing that the land is God's gift, not something Abram must seize.

Abram's generosity to Lot is faith in action. Because he trusts God to provide what was promised, he can let Lot take what looks best. Faith frees a person from the need to grasp. Lot, by contrast, chooses by appearance and for himself, and the choice will cost him dearly.

The chapter introduces Sodom with a single blunt sentence: its men were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD. The lush plain hides moral ruin, and Lot's gradual move toward the city shows how people can be drawn into evil by the attractions around it.

words.note: Parad, to separate or divide. It was used in 2:10 of the river dividing into four branches, and in 10:5 and 10:32 of the nations spreading apart. Here Abram says, separate yourself from me, and Abram and Lot part company. The separation removes the last member of Abram's father's household from the land and leaves him alone with God's promise.

Bachar, to choose. Lot chose the plain for himself (verse 11). Elsewhere the verb is used most often of God choosing Israel, a king, or a place for his name. Lot's choice is made by sight and self-interest, and the narrative lets the reader judge it by where it leads.

Kikkar, literally a round thing. It can mean a round loaf of bread, a round weight of metal (the talent), or, as here, a round plain, the broad basin of the Jordan valley. It became almost a place name for the region of the cities of the plain.

Afar, dust. It is the dust from which the man was formed (2:7) and to which humans return (3:19). Here it becomes a picture of abundance: Abram's offspring will be as countless as the dust of the earth. God will later use the stars (15:5) and the sand of the seashore (22:17) for the same promise.

christ: The land promised to Abram here becomes, in the New Testament, a pointer to something larger. Paul speaks of “the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), enlarging the land of Canaan to the whole earth, and Jesus says, “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). Abram, who gave up his right to choose and received everything from God, is an early picture of that meekness, though the Beatitude does not refer to him directly. Hebrews notes that Abraham and his family lived in the land as foreigners, in tents, because they were “longing for a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). Lot also appears in the New Testament. Peter calls him “a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless” (2 Peter 2:7), a man who belonged to God but chose to live where his soul was tormented. Paul's call to “consider others more important than yourselves” (Philippians 2:3) is lived out in advance in Abram's offer to Lot, a thematic connection rather than a direct one.

hard.q: God promises the land to Abram's offspring forever. Who inherits that promise today?
hard.a:
This question has divided Christians and has large consequences, so the main positions deserve to be stated carefully. Many Christians, especially in the dispensational tradition, hold that the promise of the land still belongs to the physical descendants of Abraham through Isaac and Jacob, and that God will fulfill it to the Jewish people in history. They stress the word forever and God's faithfulness to his word to Israel (see Romans 11:28-29). Jewish tradition likewise sees the land as part of God's lasting covenant with Israel.

Other Christians, especially in the Reformed and covenant traditions, argue that the New Testament enlarges the land promise to the whole renewed earth, inherited by all who belong to Christ, Abraham's offspring (Galatians 3:29; Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16). They note that the Old Testament itself speaks of the land promise as fulfilled under Joshua (Joshua 21:43-45) and that possession of the land was tied to covenant faithfulness. Some hold positions between these, affirming both a fulfillment in Christ and a continuing place for the Jewish people in God's purposes. All agree that God keeps his promises and that the land was always a gift, never a possession earned or seized.

questions: Abram gave Lot the first choice, trusting God to provide. Where are you tempted to insist on your rights, and what would it look like to trust God enough to yield them?
Lot chose by what looked best and slowly moved his tent toward Sodom. What attractive choices might be drawing you toward places that could harm your soul?
Wealth created conflict between two relatives who had traveled together for years. How have possessions or money strained relationships in your life, and how might you make peace?
